newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian oil seen at disadvantage in U.S. Midwest.
newsitem.headline: Canadian oil seen at disadvantage in U.S. Midwest.

text.p: Canadian oil producers face an uphill battle trying to wrest market share from competitors in the key U.S. Midwest refining region, despite large increases in pipeline capacity, an official with refiner Ashland Inc said on Tuesday.

Growing heavy and sour crude supplies from Venezuela and Mexico and those countries' investments in U.S. refineries and pipelines to secure demand are giving them a competitive edge over Canada, said Ashland vice-president of crude oil supply and trading Stephen Mawer.

A projected increase in sour production from the U.S. Gulf Coast headed for the Midwest PADD II region -- by producers with equity positions in pipelines and processing -- also threatens to unseat Canadian crude from its planned market share growth, Mawer told an oil marketing conference.
"The Canadian producer is at risk of being outmaneuvered into a low price role by the competition," he said.
Canadian producers have traditionally concentrated on boosting production as quickly and as much as possible in efforts to bring strong returns to their investors.
They have also relied on non-binding relationships to sell their increasingly heavy product to Midwest refiners, as opposed to taking equity positions in the low-return U.S. refining business.
Venezuela and Mexico, meanwhile, have made large downstream investments in the U.S., effectively boosting demand for their own production, aided by their ability to focus on the long term.
Mawer said Canadian firms would enhance their positions by providing some of the capital needed to retool lower PADD II refineries for processing their heavier crude blends.
"Competitors have similar products and they've been preparing for a market share fight for several years now. They're not afraid to commit capital if that's what needs to be done," he said.
"Clearly there are two options -- become the low-cost supplier or make strategic alliances," he said.
Ashland projections showed Canadian supplies into the U.S. were expected to grow to 1.45 million barrels per day by 2001 from 1.05 million last year.
But Latin Amrican oil was projected feed 4.3 million barrels per day of expected demand, up from 2.7 million last year.
U.S. domestic supply was projected to grow over the period to 6.9 million barrels per day from the current 6.5 million.
The one supply category projected to drop was long-haul offshore crude, which would fall to 2.25 million barrels per day from the current 3.75 million under the Ashland projection.
Mawer said another made-in-Canada barrier to market share growth in PADD II was its history of regulatory uncertainty over pipeline capacity allocation on the IPL Energy Inc system.

"The Canadian approach of not infrequent regulatory revisions, often under the behest of the group led by producers and integrated producer-refiners, makes large, long-term contractual obligations reliant on Canadian oil supply of a slightly higher risk than that from the U.S.," he said.
